body:
Different levels of political authority

Political power in the Sangam age was not exercised exclusively by the Cheras, Cholas and Pandyas. Below and alongside the great ruling families were numerous smaller chiefs, local leaders and influential landowners.

The Tamil terms ko, kon and vendar were associated with kingship. The three great ruling families are therefore collectively known as the muvendar.

Velir were minor chieftains who controlled smaller territories and could support or oppose powerful kings. The Ay chiefs were another group of local rulers. A kizhar was a village chief.

Velir refers to minor chiefs. Vellalar refers to a prominent landowning group in Tamil society. The similar-looking words describe different social positions.

How chiefs obtained and distributed wealth

Sangam poems describe chiefs receiving gifts from their followers and tribute from neighbouring areas. Military expeditions could bring cattle, goods and other valuable resources. Chiefs often kept part of the wealth and distributed the rest among relatives, warriors, poets and other supporters.

Such distribution strengthened personal loyalty. A poet who praised a ruler might receive gold, fine clothing or another valuable gift. Soldiers and followers could be rewarded for service or support.

Taxes in more developed kingdoms

Not every Sangam polity collected revenue in the same way. The NCERT description of early Tamil chiefs emphasises gifts and tribute rather than a regular system of taxation. Tamil Nadu's history textbook also describes organised royal revenue in the larger kingdoms.

For the latter, irai was a term for land revenue, and sungam referred to customs duties or tolls on traded goods. Tribute, fines and other payments could supplement these receipts.

These accounts are best understood as descriptions of different levels of political organisation. Smaller chiefdoms could depend heavily on gifts and military tribute, while larger kingdoms could maintain more regular collection of agricultural and commercial dues.

Royal administration and local divisions

The king's court was called the arasavai. The ruler was assisted by officials, and the court served as a centre for decisions, disputes and royal patronage. Tamil Nadu's textbook identifies the Aimperunguzhu, a group of 5 advisers or officials, and the Enperayam, a group of 8, as bodies assisting the ruler.

The territorial terms commonly described for the Sangam kingdoms were:

  • Mandalam: a major territorial region or kingdom.
  • Nadu: a subdivision of the larger region.
  • Kurram: a smaller subdivision.
  • Ur: a village, the basic local settlement.

The presence of these terms does not prove that administration was completely uniform in every part of Tamilakam. The scale and effectiveness of royal authority varied across localities.

Prelims focus

  • Muvendar: Chera, Chola and Pandya rulers.
  • Velir: minor chieftains; kizhar: village chief.
  • Irai: land revenue; sungam: customs or tolls.
  • Arasavai: royal court.
  • Mandalam, nadu, kurram and ur: territorial terms from larger unit to village.
  • Trap: The statement that some chiefs relied on gifts does not mean that all Sangam kings collected no taxes.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 10, pp. 100–101; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 2, p. 35; Tamil Nadu SCERT, Social Science, Class 6, Term III, History Unit 1, pp. 90–93, 2018 edition, consulted 18 November 2026; IGNOU, India: 200 BCE to 300 CE, Unit 4, Section 4.5, consulted 18 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Chiefs redistributed gifts and tribute; larger kingdoms also collected irai and sungam to support rulers, officials, soldiers and patronage.
pictures.caption: Gifts and tribute supported chiefs, while larger kingdoms also collected land revenue and customs.

title: Sangam Kingship, Local Chiefs and Revenue

body:
The five tinai landscapes

A distinctive feature of early Tamil literature is the classification of the natural environment into 5 tinai, or ecological and poetic landscapes. Each tinai was associated with particular landforms, livelihoods, plants, traditions and deities.

The classification connects physical geography with social and cultural life. It is not an exact map with fixed borders: real settlements could contain overlapping features, and the tinai also functioned as a poetic convention.

TinaiLandscapeCharacteristic livelihoodAssociated deity
KurinjiMountains and hillsHunting, gathering and hill cultivationMurugan or Seyon
MullaiPastures and woodlandsCattle rearing and pastoral lifeMayon
MarutamFertile river plainsPlough agriculture, especially paddyIndra or Vendan
NeitalCoasts and adjoining watersFishing, pearl fishing and salt makingVaruna
PalaiParched or arid landTravel, warrior activity and cattle raidingKorravai

Marutam was especially important for settled wet-field agriculture. Its fertile fields were called menpulam and supported crops such as paddy and sugarcane. Less fertile tracts supported a variety of dry grains, pulses and other crops.

Palai is particularly important as a distinction. It represented a parched landscape and could reflect seasonal drying of other areas. It should not automatically be understood as a permanently separate desert region.

Landowners, cultivators and labourers

Early Tamil society was not composed of people with equal access to land or wealth. Sangam literature distinguishes different groups engaged in agricultural production.

  • Vellalar: substantial landowners or a prominent landholding group.
  • Uzhavar: ploughmen and cultivators who worked agricultural fields.
  • Kadaisiyar: landless agricultural labourers.
  • Adimai: enslaved persons who could be made to perform labour.

These distinctions show that the same agricultural economy contained landowners, working cultivators and people dependent on others for their livelihood.

Occupations beyond farming

Fishing communities obtained fish, pearls and other marine products from coastal waters. Salt makers produced salt that could be exchanged for grain from inland areas. Herders kept cattle, while artisans worked as weavers, carpenters, blacksmiths, potters and goldsmiths.

This variety of occupations encouraged local exchange between different ecological regions. A coastal household might need paddy from the river plains, while an inland village might obtain salt from the coast.

Religion, poetry and public memory

Sangam literature refers to the worship of Murugan, Mayon, Indra, Varuna and Korravai in different cultural settings. Buddhist and Jain traditions were also present in the wider region.

A nadukal, also called a virakkal or hero stone, commemorated a warrior or another person remembered for heroic action. Such stones reflect the importance assigned to courage and remembrance in early Tamil society.

Poets and performers held important places in cultural life. Panar were singing bards. Music, dance and public performances formed part of social and courtly culture. Women also participated in literary production; Avvaiyar is among the well-known women poets associated with the early Tamil poetic tradition.

Prelims focus

  • Kurinji: hills; Mullai: pastoral woodland; Marutam: fertile plains.
  • Neital: coast and fishing; Palai: parched land and travel.
  • Menpulam: fertile agricultural land, especially associated with Marutam.
  • Vellalar: substantial landowners; uzhavar: ploughmen.
  • Nadukal or virakkal: a memorial hero stone.
  • Trap: The 5 tinai are ecological and poetic categories, not 5 separate political kingdoms.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 9, pp. 88–89; Tamil Nadu SCERT, Social Science, Class 6, Term III, History Unit 1, pp. 93–95, 2018 edition, consulted 18 November 2026; IGNOU, India: 200 BCE to 300 CE, Unit 4, Sections 4.3–4.5, pp. 64–69, consulted 18 November 2026.]

title: Sangam Landscapes, Society and Cultural Life

body:
Trade within Tamilakam

Trade in the Sangam age took place at local, regional and overseas levels. Farming communities, fishing settlements, pastoral groups and towns produced different goods. Merchants linked them by moving surplus products from one area to another.

Barter, or the direct exchange of one good for another without money, was common. Sangam poetry describes merchants transporting salt from the coast and exchanging it for paddy produced inland.

Barter did not exclude the use of coins. Coins also circulated in the wider economy, especially in commercial and urban settings. Thus, the existence of barter should not lead to the conclusion that the Sangam economy had no monetary exchange.

Major ports and overseas exchange

The western and eastern coasts provided access to different maritime networks. Muziris on the western coast was important for overseas commerce and the spice trade. Puhar on the eastern coast connected the Chola region with maritime traders. Korkai, linked with the Pandyas, was particularly associated with the pearl trade.

A Sangam poem describing Puhar refers to goods arriving from several regions, including horses, pepper, gems, gold, sandalwood, pearls, coral and agricultural products. Its description indicates the wide range of merchandise collected in an active port city.

Exports and imports

Products exported from the Tamil region included pepper, pearls, spices, fine textiles, ivory and precious stones. Imports and goods arriving through overseas trade included wine, horses, metals, glassware and luxury pottery. The direction of trade depended on the commodity and the particular route.

Pepper was especially valuable in Mediterranean markets. The demand for spices, gems, textiles and pearls encouraged commercial contacts between Indian ports and the Roman world.

Arikamedu and contact with the Roman world

Arikamedu, near present-day Puducherry, was a coastal settlement connected with overseas trade. Finds described in the textbooks include amphorae, large double-handled containers commonly used to transport liquids such as wine or oil, and Arretine ware, a type of fine Roman red pottery.

Other evidence includes glass objects, beads and locally produced items. These finds show that imported merchandise reached the Tamil coast and that local craft activity existed alongside overseas commerce.

Arikamedu is a trade-related coastal settlement. Puhar, Muziris and Korkai are associated with the Chola, Chera and Pandya commercial networks respectively. Evidence of Roman goods at a site is not proof that it was a Roman political colony.

How the Deccan and Tamilakam differed

The Satavahanas and the Sangam polities were part of the same broad age of expanding regional states and trade, but their political centres, languages and economic settings differed.

FeatureSatavahana DeccanSangam Tamilakam
Main political organisationSatavahana monarchy with regional chiefs and officersChera, Chola and Pandya ruling families with smaller chiefs
Important placesPratishthana, Naneghat, Nashik and AmaravatiMadurai, Uraiyur, Puhar, Muziris and Korkai
Important literary languagePrakrit in royal inscriptions and literary worksTamil in Sangam poetry and early inscriptions
Major sources of wealthAgriculture, inland routes, trade and taxationRiver-valley agriculture, gifts, tribute, taxes and coastal trade
Distinctive cultural evidenceRoyal inscriptions, religious grants and Buddhist monumentsSangam poetry, tinai traditions and hero stones

The comparison must not hide their connections. Both regions supported specialised occupations, benefited from long-distance exchange, and developed towns and religious or cultural institutions. Both also contained significant differences in wealth and social standing.

Prelims focus

  • Muziris: western coastal port associated with the Cheras and overseas trade.
  • Puhar: Chola port on the eastern coast.
  • Korkai: Pandya port associated with pearls.
  • Arikamedu: coastal trading site near Puducherry with Roman-linked pottery.
  • Amphora: a large transport container; Arretine ware: fine Roman red pottery.
  • Trap: Bharuch or Barygaza is in Gujarat; Arikamedu is near Puducherry. They are different trading sites.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 9, pp. 91–98, and Chapter 10, pp. 99–102; Tamil Nadu SCERT, Social Science, Class 6, Term III, History Unit 1, pp. 95–96, 2018 edition, consulted 18 November 2026; IGNOU, India: 200 BCE to 300 CE, Unit 4, Sections 4.4–4.5, consulted 18 November 2026; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 2, pp. 35–36.]
